chess.lede:
<!--@chess.lede-->A real chess board that plays you by itself. A sensor grid reads the
                 positions and a CoreXY gantry carries an electromagnet beneath the board.
                 H.G. Muller's micro-Max engine, adapted and retrofitted for the machine, runs
                 natively on an Arduino with no computer in the loop.<!--/@-->
chess.sensors-intro:
Under each square is a Hall effect sensor detecting pieces, which passes what it
                 sees to the Arduino, which then moves the opposing pieces using the CoreXY gantry.
chess.access: Built to be played with. Difficulty is adjustable through search depth, so a beginner and a stronger player get a game rather than a formality. An LED matrix under the board lights the legal moves for a piece you pick up, and the moves the engine would consider best, which turns a game into a lesson. And every move is announced aloud, so someone who can't easily read a board across the table can still follow the game.
chess.awards: Provincial finalist, Hydro-Québec Science Fair. OIQ (Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec) award for technical complexity, OCTAS Youth Innovation award, and a Université de Sherbrooke scholarship.
chess.revisions:
<!--@chess.revisions-->Across 18 months I prototyped three complete systems to reach a working
                 board. Real geometry below, straight from the CAD.<!--/@-->
chess.learned: What I had to work out System integration and electronics packaging. It was the first time I'd worked under so many constraints at once. Motors, drivers, and the electromagnet itself all threw electromagnetic interference across the sensor grid. Wiring, calibrating, and reading 64 individual sensors was its own problem, and came to over 40 m of wire. Shielding was added to all motor and sensor signal wires. Each sensor was calibrated with no interference, and with magnets. Electronics packaging was managed by adding components to all surfaces, including below the hinging playing surface.
chess.movement:
<!--@chess.movement-->CoreXY is a compact but more complex way to get cartesian movement,
                 commonly used in 3D printers. Both motors stay bolted to the frame, so none of
                 their weight moves. The trade is that neither one drives X or Y on its own, since
                 every move is a combination of the two. Drag the magnet, or drive one motor at a
                 time.<!--/@-->
chess.corexy-note:
<svg viewBox="0 0 26 14" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1 11 C 8 12, 16 8, 23 3 M23 3 L17 4 M23 3 L22 9"/></svg>
                one motor alone gives a diagonal, which is the whole idea
chess.sensing:
<!--@chess.sensing-->Under each square is a Hall effect sensor, which detects not only
                 that a piece is there but also its polarity. Each one has three pins. Power and
                 ground sit on shared rails, so only the signal leg is unique, and the 64 signals
                 fan into four 16-channel multiplexers before reaching the Arduino. Hover a square
                 to follow its path.<!--/@-->
chess.mux-note:
<svg viewBox="0 0 26 14" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1 11 C 8 12, 16 8, 23 3 M23 3 L17 4 M23 3 L22 9"/></svg>
                the select lines are shared, so all four mux read the same channel at once
chess.engine: The chess itself is a minimax engine by H.G. Muller, retrofitted for my own chess board's needs: difficulty through search depth, an LED grid for legal moves, and an LED grid for best moves.
chess.engine-tree:
The algorithm calculates moves in a tree to see which future branch awards it the
                 most advantage, while minimising the opponent's.
chess.heat-note:
Brighter squares are ones the search

crc.lede:
<!--@crc.lede-->Over the course of 8 months, I developed the robot for John
                 Abbott's robotics team, competing in the Canadian Robotics Competition. I built a
                 swerve drive drivetrain, and a dual claw mechanism to both stack and move game
                 pieces, movable in all three axes independently from the drive base.<!--/@-->
crc.award: These ideas placed us 2nd for Robot Design.
crc.swerve-what:
A swerve drive is a powered wheel that can steer in all 360 degrees. Syncing the
                 steering and drive of all four wheels lets the robot drive in any direction
                 without changing its orientation.
crc.swap: Designed to be swapped, not repaired. Each module is self-contained and held in by just four bolts. Take them out and the whole module drops out from below, and a fresh one goes in the same way.
crc.claw:
The claw doesn't grip. Two arms on fixed pivots act like chopsticks: each
                 one stays tangent to the game piece, one on either side, so swinging them pushes
                 the piece side to side while it's held from both directions the whole way.
                 The game scores a multiplier for stacked pieces, so placement has to be exact.
                 The chopstick motion adds extra movement in the Y direction on its own, lining a
                 piece up over the stack while the base stays still.
                 Drag the piece, or grab either arm.

rl.lede:
<!--@rl.lede-->This is the balance and driving controller for my wheel-leg biped.
                 Instead of tuning a controller by hand, I trained a neural network in the MuJoCo
                 simulator using reinforcement learning (PPO). Training took about 25 million
                 control steps, which works out to 69 hours of simulated driving.<!--/@-->
rl.demo:
<!--@rl.demo-->The player below replays the trained policy in simulation. The network
                 next to it is the actual trained network. Its 22,406 weights run in your browser
                 on the same sensor readings the simulated robot received, so the neurons lighting
                 up are the ones deciding each motor command. The clips marked Demo mode use a
                 second policy trained with the hardware limits removed, described at the end of
                 this section.<!--/@-->
rl.network:
<!--@rl.network-->Every 10 ms the network takes 39 values and returns 6. It has no
                 memory between steps and no physics model. It is two hidden layers of 128
                 neurons with tanh activations, mapping the current state directly to motor
                 commands.<!--/@-->
rl.hips-note:
The hips are position controlled. A PD loop running at 1 kHz
                     converts each target into a torque, through a 12:1 3D printed planetary
                     gearbox. The wheels are commanded in torque directly. The wheels do the
                     balancing, and the legs set the ride height and absorb uneven ground.
rl.norm:
<!--@rl.norm-->The inputs are normalized using statistics collected during training, and
                 the network only works with those exact statistics. If the weights are exported
                 without them, the export still passes its own check but the robot behaves
                 incorrectly. This happened once, so the export script now refuses to run
                 without the matching statistics file.<!--/@-->
rl.export:
<!--@rl.export-->The weights are also exported to a C header for the microcontroller. I
                 checked the C version of the forward pass against the Python network, and the
                 outputs match to within 4×10<sup>−7</sup>.<!--/@-->
rl.ppo:
<!--@rl.ppo-->PPO trains the network from experience. Six copies of the simulator
                 run in parallel, the policy drives each one, and every control step receives a
                 reward. After each batch, the network is updated toward the actions that did
                 better than expected. PPO limits how far a single update can change the policy,
                 which keeps training stable.<!--/@-->
rl.curriculum:
<!--@rl.curriculum-->Training uses a curriculum. It starts on flat ground with an ideal
                 robot that is mostly asked to stand still. Over the first 40% of training, the
                 terrain gets rougher, the pushes get stronger, and the robot's physical
                 parameters are randomized over wider ranges.<!--/@-->
rl.learned: What I had to work out The most useful habit was checking why episodes ended, not only how long they lasted. Partway through one run, episode length dropped from 1860 to 1160 steps. It looked like the normal dip when the curriculum gets harder, but it was a bug. The crouch command limit had been calculated from nominal motor values, and once the randomization widened, 92.5% of the simulated robots could not physically hold the commanded pose. A second bug computed the velocity reward in the world frame instead of the robot's frame, so it measured the wrong axis whenever the robot turned. Forward speed tracking was stuck at 52% of the command until I fixed it.
rl.sim2real:
<!--@rl.sim2real-->A policy trained on one perfect simulated robot will not work on the
                 real one, so the simulation is made harder than reality on purpose. The motor
                 model uses the measured electrical constants, with a back-EMF torque limit and a
                 1 A current limit, and the windings heat up with use. Each episode also uses a
                 different randomized robot.<!--/@-->
rl.status: Current status The controller is not finished. Under nominal conditions it balances, drives, turns in place and recovers from pushes. Turn rate tracks within a few percent, but forward speed only reaches about two thirds of a fast command, which you can see on the speed gauge in the player. It also does not follow ride height commands yet. With full randomization it still fails about half of its 20 second episodes, and it cannot reliably drive off an 18 mm step. The next steps are validation in simulation, then testing on the real robot.
rl.demo-lede:
<!--@rl.demo-lede-->The policy above is limited by what my hardware can do. For this
                 version I continued training the same policy in a simulation with the physical
                 limits removed, to see how far the method could go when motor power was not the
                 constraint. It appears as the Demo mode clips in the player. It is only a
                 simulation result and will not be used on the real robot.<!--/@-->
rl.demo-result:
<!--@rl.demo-result-->I trained it for another 8 million steps, which took 3.5 hours. It
                 turns at 5.8 rad/s when asked for 6.0, stays up after 1 m/s pushes, and drives
                 over 24 mm steps. The hardware-limited policy fell on 18 mm steps in all
                 8 test runs. Episode survival went from about 50% to 81%.<!--/@-->
rl.demo-limits: What did not improve More power did not fix everything. Forward speed still undershoots, reaching 1.24 m/s when asked for 1.8, and it still ignores ride height commands. The hardware-limited policy has both of these problems too, so they are not caused by a lack of torque. A push that lands while it is driving and turning at the same time still knocks it over in five of six runs.
